# Abstract

The post-colonial territorial reorganisation of northwestern and eastern South Asia following the August 1947 Partition of British India established one of the most volatile demographic landscapes of the twentieth century. Encompassing 981.558 km² of terrestrial surface across 13.375 active 5-arcminute grid cells, the domain analysed under INDUS incorporates the sovereign territories of Pakistan alongside the 1947 to 1971 territorial bridge of East Pakistan prior to the birth of Bangladesh. Across eight decades spanning from 1947AD to 2026AD, this geographic sphere absorbed catastrophic cross-border refugee migrations, fought three major interstate wars in 1947, 1965 and 1971, endured the influx of over three million Afghan refugees following the 1979 Soviet intervention, achieved strategic nuclear deterrence in 1998, and underwent an extraordinary demographic expansion from 73M inhabitants at independence to 254M by 2026AD.

In August 1947, the partition of British India ignited an unprecedented demographic convulsion, displacing 14M to 15M individuals across newly demarcated international borders. Approximately 7,2M Muslim refugees entered West and East Pakistan, while roughly equal numbers of Hindus and Sikhs evacuated to India. This traumatic exchange concentrated immense refugee masses within major urban centres: Karachi expanded from 400k in 1947 to 1,06M in the 1951 census, transforming an arid provincial port into an industrial metropolis dominated by Urdu-speaking Muhajir communities. Simultaneously, cities across West Punjab such as Lahore (849k in 1951), Faisalabad (179k in 1951), Multan and Rawalpindi absorbed massive displaced populations while coping with the abrupt departure of commercial and professional minorities. Across the united Pakistan state, population expanded from 73M in 1947AD to 75,84M in 1951AD and 93,72M by 1961AD, reaching 129M at the onset of 1971AD.

The climactic crisis of March to December 1971 produced a fundamental structural rupture in South Asian political geography. Following severe political alienation, economic disparities and the military crackdown of Operation Searchlight, the Bangladesh Liberation War and subsequent third Indo-Pakistani war precipitated the flight of roughly 10M refugees into neighbouring Indian border states. The surrender of Pakistani armed forces in Dhaka on 16 December 1971 resulted in the formal secession of East Pakistan and the creation of sovereign Bangladesh. In the demographic time series, this event registers as a sharp structural dislocation: total population within the residual sovereign territory of Pakistan stepped down to 65,31M in the 1972 census. Over subsequent decades, rapid natural increase and rural-to-urban migration propelled Pakistan to 84,25M in 1981AD, 132,35M in 1998AD, 207,68M in 2017AD, 241,5M in 2023AD, and 254M in 2026AD.

This study reconstructs the quantitative demography of the five constituent conflict-theatre divisions by coupling longitudinal census records from 1951, 1961, 1972, 1981, 1998, 2017 and 2023 with 845 georeferenced urban settlement trajectories. By deducting catalogued municipal populations from sub-regional envelopes, the analysis achieves a balanced dasymetric distribution of rural cultivators across canal-irrigated doabs, arid rangelands and deltaic wetlands. The results illustrate how interstate border conflicts, forced migrations and massive infrastructure developments, notably the Indus Waters Treaty link canals and Tarbela and Mangla dams, reshaped settlement densities across northwestern South Asia over the post-colonial epoch.

# Background

## The 1947 Partition and Demography of Mass Displacement

The boundary decisions formulated by Sir Cyril Radcliffe in August 1947 bisected the historic provinces of Punjab and Bengal, terminating British imperial sovereignty while creating two non-contiguous wings of Pakistan separated by over 1.600 kilometres of Indian territory [@Spate1947Partitio; @Brooks1947Partitio]. The demarcation disregarded long-established canal irrigation infrastructure, rail corridors and demographic contiguities, generating instant minority populations that faced acute existential jeopardy amidst communal violence [@Chattha2022Communal; @Pardesi2019Violent]. In Punjab, the breakdown of civil administration and the politicisation of local police forces precipitated reciprocal communal massacres, triggering total panic and spontaneous mass flight across the new border [@Chattha2022Communal; @Iqbal2026Forced].

The Punjab Partition Committee, convened during July and August 1947, sought to negotiate an orderly transfer of administrative assets, civil servants and security equipment [@BANGASH2021Implemen]. However, the velocity of violence overwhelmed official arrangements. Foot columns (kafilas) stretching for tens of kilometres, packed refugee trains (often subjected to ambushes) and military-escorted convoys transported millions of exhausted peasants across the boundary line [@Iqbal2026Forced; @Mubasshir2024Partitio]. By late 1948, West Punjab had absorbed over 5,3M Muslim refugees, primarily originating from East Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh, while roughly 4,4M Hindus and Sikhs departed for India [@Iqbal2026Forced; @Kong2021Christia]. This transfer altered the ethnolinguistic composition of the central Punjab doabs, replacing Sikh and Hindu landholders with incoming cultivators who were assigned evacuee property under complex rehabilitation schemes.

In Bengal, the partition dynamic assumed a markedly distinct structural character [@Pardesi2019Violent; @Batabyal2014Review]. Unlike the rapid and almost total mutual expulsion observed in Punjab within a few catastrophic months, displacement across the East Pakistan and West Bengal frontier unfolded in protracted, episodic pulses across several decades [@Paul2020Experien; @Batabyal2014Review]. While initial communal rioting in Noakhali and Calcutta in 1946 stimulated early cross-border movements, large rural populations, particularly Scheduled Caste (Namashudra) cultivators, remained on their ancestral lands in East Bengal [@Barman2009Partitio; @Banerjee2017Differen; @Sarkar2024Bandyopa]. Waves of communal tension in 1950, 1954 and 1964 triggered successive migration pulses into West Bengal, Assam and Tripura, generating persistent refugee settlement friction across the delta [@Banerjee2024Trauma; @Sayyada2025Politics]. Concurrently, Urdu-speaking Muslim migrants from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, numbering approximately one million, settled in urban enclaves across East Pakistan, including Dhaka, Saidpur and Chittagong, creating an unassimilated linguistic minority that subsequently faced severe political vulnerability in 1971 [@Paul2020Experien; @Zahra2026Secessioni].

In the western wing, the urban impact of partition was most pronounced in Sindh and its provincial capital, Karachi [@Priyanka2022Literature]. In 1947, Karachi was a modest coastal trading port of approximately 400k inhabitants, where Sindhi Hindus constituted over half the municipality and dominated commerce, finance and civil administration. The arrival of over 600k Urdu-speaking Muhajirs from the United Provinces, Delhi, Bombay and Hyderabad Deccan completely transformed the city's demography [@Priyanka2022Literature]. By the 1951 census, Karachi reached 1,06M inhabitants, of whom over 57% were refugees. This rapid influx established a stark demographic dichotomy between an urbanised, Urdu-speaking commercial and bureaucratic core in Karachi and Hyderabad, and a rural, Sindhi-speaking agrarian hinterland governed by traditional landowning elites (waderas).

## The Indus Waters Treaty and Agricultural Resettlement

The partition boundary bisected the world's most intricate contiguous irrigation network: the canal colonies of Punjab, developed by British engineers from the 1880s onward [@Spate1947Partitio; @Brooks1947Partitio]. The international border placed the headworks of key Pakistani canal systems, such as the Upper Bari Doab Canal at Madhopur on the Ravi and the Dipalpur Canal at Ferozepore on the Sutlej, under Indian sovereign control. In April 1948, Indian authorities temporarily halted canal diversions to downstream Pakistani watercourses, exposing the severe vulnerability of millions of hectares of prime agrarian land in Lahore, Sahiwal and Multan.

A decade of protracted technical negotiations, mediated by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank), culminated in the signing of the Indus Waters Treaty in September 1960. The treaty allocated the waters of the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas and Sutlej) exclusively to India after a transitional period, while assigning the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum and Chenab) to Pakistan. To compensate for the loss of eastern river flows, Pakistan initiated the massive Indus Basin Replacement Works programme, constructing eight inter-river link canals, several major barrages and two monumental storage reservoirs: Mangla Dam on the Jhelum River (completed in 1967) and Tarbela Dam on the Indus River (completed in 1976).

This hydraulic reconfiguration reshaped regional settlement patterns. The link canals transferred vast volumes of water from the northern rivers southward across the Chaj and Rechna doabs, stabilising agricultural production in canal colony districts such as Faisalabad, Jhang and Bahawalpur, and fostering rapid demographic densification. Conversely, the construction of Mangla Dam flooded over 260 km² of fertile land in the Mirpur district of Azad Kashmir, displacing approximately 110k individuals. A substantial proportion of these displaced families utilised cash compensation and official resettlement vouchers to migrate to the United Kingdom, establishing a diaspora that maintained profound demographic and financial links with the Kashmir borderland through remittances that fueled local construction booms in Mirpur and Kotli.

## The 1965 War and Western Border Confrontations

Tensions over the contested princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, partitioned by the 1948 Ceasefire Line (CFL) following the first Indo-Pakistani conflict, erupted into open warfare in 1965 [@Diyun2024Kashmir; @Yaseen2016Pakistan]. Preliminary skirmishes in the salt marshes of the Rann of Kutch during early 1965 escalated in August when Pakistan launched Operation Gibraltar, dispatching covert paramilitary forces across the Ceasefire Line into the Kashmir Valley, followed by Operation Grand Slam, an armoured thrust toward Akhnoor aimed at severing Indian communications in Jammu [@Yaseen2016Pakistan; @Sabar2022Indo].

India responded on 6 September 1965 by launching a counter-offensive across the international border in Punjab, advancing toward Lahore along the Grand Trunk Road and opening a secondary front in the Sialkot sector. For three weeks, intense armoured and artillery engagements raged within sight of the suburbs of Lahore, notably around the BRB (Bambawali-Ravi-Bedian) Canal, and at the Battle of Chawinda near Sialkot, representing the largest tank battle since the Second World War. The conflict caused extensive localised civilian displacement along the border tehsils of Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot and Gujrat, where hundreds of thousands of villagers evacuated toward inner canal towns.

The war terminated on 23 September 1965 under United Nations Security Council auspices, followed by the Soviet-mediated Tashkent Declaration in January 1966, which mandated the restoration of pre-war territorial boundaries [@Kumar2021Russia]. While territorial boundaries remained unaltered, the 1965 war carried profound demographic and political ramifications. In East Pakistan, the complete physical isolation of the province during hostilities, defended by only a single infantry division while central authorities focused resources entirely on the western front, crystallized Bengali perceptions of strategic abandonment and economic neglect, providing potent momentum to regional autonomy movements [@Zahra2026Secessioni; @Ulfat2023Sheikh].

## The 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War and Demographic Fracture

The political crisis that culminated in the 1971 war was rooted in structural asymmetries between West and East Pakistan [@Zahra2026Secessioni; @Taib2022Media]. Although East Pakistan contained 54% of the national population in the 1961 census (50,84M inhabitants compared to 42,88M in West Pakistan), the political, military and bureaucratic apparatus remained heavily concentrated in West Punjab and Karachi. Revenue generated from East Pakistani jute and tea exports was disproportionately allocated to western industrialisation and defence expenditures, while Bengali political demands for cultural and linguistic parity encountered institutional resistance [@Taib2022Media; @Zahra2026Secessioni].

The catastrophic Bhola cyclone of November 1970, which killed an estimated 300k to 500k people across the coastal islands of the Meghna estuary, exposed the administrative paralysis of the central government, deepening regional disaffection. Weeks later, in the December 1970 general election, the Awami League, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on a platform of provincial autonomy (the Six-Point Programme), won a landslide victory, securing 160 of the 162 general seats allocated to East Pakistan and an absolute majority in the national assembly [@Ulfat2023Sheikh]. The refusal of the military regime and western political leaders to transfer sovereign authority precipitated widespread civil disobedience across the province.

On 25 March 1971, the Pakistan armed forces initiated Operation Searchlight, launching systematic military operations across Dhaka, Chittagong and major district centres to crush Bengali political mobilisations [@Sen2022Martyrs; @Sarkar2024Indian]. Over the subsequent nine months, intense violence engulfed towns and villages throughout East Bengal. Intellectuals, students, political workers and members of the Hindu minority were targeted, resulting in widespread fatalities, infrastructural destruction and mass displacement [@Sen2022Martyrs; @Diyun2024Kashmir].

The resulting humanitarian catastrophe precipitated the flight of roughly 10M refugees across the porous 4.000-kilometre border into India, representing one of the largest sudden refugee migrations in modern history [@Sarkar2024Indian; @Diyun2024Kashmir]. Over 7M refugees were housed in official camps established by the Indian government in West Bengal, with additional concentrations in Tripura, Assam and Meghalaya [@Sarkar2024Indian]. The demographic strain on Indian public finances and civic administration was profound, prompting Indian strategic planners to provide military training and logistical sanctuary to the Bengali guerrilla resistance, the Mukti Bahini [@Sarkar2024Indian].

Following preemptive Pakistani airstrikes on Indian airbases on 3 December 1971, full-scale war erupted across both fronts [@Diyun2024Kashmir]. In the western theatre, engagements took place along the Line of Control in Kashmir and across the Punjab and Sindh borders, including the Battle of Longewala in the Thar Desert and naval operations off Karachi harbour [@Yaseen2016Pakistan; @Sabar2022Indo]. In the eastern theatre, a coordinated multi-pronged advance by the Indian Army and Mukti Bahini outmanoeuvred Pakistani defensive strongpoints, reaching Dhaka within two weeks. On 16 December 1971, the commander of Pakistani forces in the east signed the instrument of surrender, concluding the conflict and securing the sovereign establishment of Bangladesh. The partition of 1971 severed 55% of Pakistan's demographic mass, reducing the country's population from 129M in early 1971 to 65,31M in the 1972 census, and permanently dissolving the post-1947 two-wing constitutional structure [@Zahra2026Secessioni].

## Afghan Refugee Influx and Western Frontier Transformation

Less than a decade after the traumatic loss of East Pakistan, the geopolitical landscape along Pakistan's western border was upended by the December 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan [@Yaseen2016Pakistan]. The resulting counter-insurgency warfare and economic disruption triggered a mass exodus of Afghan civilians across the Durand Line into Pakistan. Between 1979 and 1989, over 3,2M registered Afghan refugees entered Pakistan, with hundreds of thousands more entering without formal registration.

The demographic weight of this influx fell almost entirely upon two provinces: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (then North-West Frontier Province), which accommodated approximately 68% of the refugees, and Balochistan, which received roughly 25%, with smaller numbers moving southward to Karachi. Across the Peshawar valley, Kohat, Bannu and the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), over 300 refugee tent villages (RTVs) coalesced into permanent mud-brick settlements, radically expanding the human footprint in water-scarce upland catchments. In Balochistan, massive refugee concentrations around Quetta, Pishin and Chaman transformed local demographic balances, shifting the provincial ratio between ethnic Pashtuns and Baloch communities.

The prolonged presence of Afghan refugees altered regional transport corridors, commercial trade networks and labor markets. While repatriation programmes facilitated the return of millions of Afghans following the fall of the Taliban regime in 2001, substantial populations remained in Pakistan across second- and third-generation cohorts, sustaining elevated population baselines in peripheral frontier districts into the 2020s.

## Nuclearisation, the Line of Control and Modern Urban Expansion

The strategic balance in South Asia was decisively militarised in May 1998, when Pakistan conducted six underground nuclear tests in the Ras Koh Hills and Kharan Desert of Balochistan in response to Indian nuclear tests at Pokhran [@Harjeet2021Asian]. Nuclear parity introduced strategic deterrence between the two rivals, preventing large-scale conventional armored warfare across the Punjab plains but failing to suppress low-intensity conflict along the Line of Control (LoC) in Kashmir [@Harjeet2021Asian; @Diyun2024Kashmir].

In the summer of 1999, the Kargil conflict witnessed intense high-altitude mountain warfare along the Line of Control in northern Jammu and Kashmir, after Pakistani paramilitary forces and northern light infantry occupied fortified ridgelines commanding the Srinagar-Leh highway [@Diyun2024Kashmir; @Sabar2022Indo]. The confrontation resulted in extensive civilian displacement from border villages in Kargil, Dras, Skardu and Gultari before intense diplomatic pressure, mediated by the United States, prompted a Pakistani withdrawal to the status quo ante [@Sabar2022Indo]. Periodic cross-border artillery duels and skirmishes along the LoC and Working Boundary continued across the 2000s and 2010s, maintaining militarised buffer zones along border tehsils in Azad Kashmir and Sialkot.

Concurrently, the internal demography of Pakistan experienced relentless urbanisation and spatial concentration. In Punjab, an interconnected industrial corridor coalesced along the Grand Trunk Road and motorways connecting Lahore (12,44M in 2025), Gujranwala (2,27M), Sialkot (655k), Faisalabad (3,58M) and Rawalpindi (2,35M) with the federal capital, Islamabad (1,9M, founded in 1960). In Sindh, Karachi expanded into a global megacity surpassing 20M inhabitants, anchoring international commerce, banking and maritime transport while absorbing millions of internal migrants from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and rural Sindh. These metropolitan growth corridors created massive agglomeration economies while straining civic infrastructure, municipal water supplies and urban transport systems [@Dahar2017Impact; @Ahmed2023Brics; @Ullah2021Comparison].

# Methodology

## Spatial Partitioning and Conflict-Theatre Geometries

To systematically analyse the demographic evolution of Pakistan and the historic 1947 to 1971 East Pakistan theatre, the INDUS spatial engine partitions the 981.558 km² study domain into 13.375 active 5-arcminute terrestrial grid cells (measuring approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). The domain is disaggregated into five conflict-theatre divisions that capture distinct historical, ecological and strategic dynamics:
1. West Punjab and Islamabad (203.722 km², 2.783 active cells): The historic core of post-colonial Pakistan, encompassing the fertile canal-irrigated doabs between the Indus and Ravi rivers, the federal capital territory of Islamabad, and the heavily fortified western confrontation zone along the international border with India.
2. Sindh and Karachi (139.911 km², 1.825 active cells): The lower Indus alluvial plain and Arabian Sea littoral, encompassing the primary post-1947 Muhajir resettlement corridor, the industrial megacity of Karachi, secondary urban hubs in Hyderabad and Sukkur, and extensive barrage-fed cotton and rice tracts.
3. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan (440.519 km², 5.929 active cells): The expansive arid and mountainous western frontier, encompassing the Sulaiman and Hindu Kush ranges, the Khyber and Bolan passes, the rugged rangelands of Balochistan, and the primary reception zone for millions of Afghan refugees from 1979 onward.
4. Kashmir Line of Control Theatre (63.816 km², 1.109 active cells): The contested northern mountainous territory administered by Pakistan, encompassing Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan and the highly militarised confrontation perimeter along the Line of Control and Siachen Glacier.
5. East Pakistan and 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War Theatre (133.590 km², 1.729 active cells): The humid deltaic plain of Bengal between the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers, tracked as an integral constitutional wing of Pakistan from 1947AD until its sovereign secession following the liberation war of 1971AD.

## Dasymetric Allocation and Settlement Subtraction

To eliminate artificial double counting between expanding urban agglomerations and rural agricultural populations, 845 catalogued settlements with longitudinal census series spanning from 1951 to 2025 are anchored to their exact WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each decadal benchmark year (1947, 1951, 1961, 1971, 1972, 1981, 1998, 2017, 2023 and 2026), the active population of catalogued urban settlements within each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining non-settled rural population is allocated across non-settled terrestrial cells utilizing dasymetric weighting layers calibrated to local agricultural carrying capacity:
- Fluvial and canal proximity: High weighting assigned to cells within 10 kilometres of perennial river channels (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi) and major canal links (BRB Canal, Chashma-Jhelum Link, Taunsa-Panjnad Link), reflecting intensive irrigated agriculture.
- Terrain slope: Topographic penalty applied to steep terrain across the Sulaiman, Salt, Karakoram and Hindu Kush ranges, channeling rural cultivators into valley floors and alluvial fans.
- Bioclimatic aridity: Exponential density attenuation across hyper-arid tracts of the Thar Desert, Cholistan and Chagai-Kharan uplands lacking surface irrigation infrastructure.
- Deltaic flood risk: Controlled weightings across the lower Bengal delta and Indus delta to account for seasonal monsoonal inundations and mangrove swamps.

## Census Reconstruction and Post-1971 Demographic Disaggregation

Official demographic figures are compiled from the seven national censuses conducted in Pakistan: 1951, 1961, 1972 (delayed from 1971 due to war), 1981, 1998, 2017 and 2023, alongside verified pre-independence 1941 census baselines and 2026 projections. For East Pakistan, the 1951 and 1961 Pakistan census tabulations are integrated directly with pre-war 1971 estimates formulated prior to Operation Searchlight.

The structural break of 1971 is modeled through an explicit territorial decoupling between December 1971 and the 1972 census. Prior to December 1971, headline national figures encompass both wings, reaching 129M at the 1971 benchmark. Following the formal independence of Bangladesh, the 1972 census benchmark records only the residual population of West Pakistan (65,31M). To maintain analytical continuity across the 1947 to 2026 trajectory, the East Pakistan territorial module is reported in all sub-regional tables as a separate conflict-theatre series, illustrating both the united 1947 to 1971 union and subsequent sovereign trajectories.

## Uncertainty Intervals and Borderland Constraints

Every benchmark estimate in the INDUS reconstruction carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty interval (+/- 4% in West Punjab, Sindh and East Pakistan; +/- 6% to +/- 8% in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and Kashmir). These envelopes accommodate documented historical variances:
- Under-enumeration in early post-colonial censuses, particularly regarding women and infants in rural purdah households.
- Fluid cross-border refugee mobility during the 1947 Partition and the 1971 Liberation War, where millions moved outside formal registration mechanisms.
- Disputed enumeration tallies in the 2017 and 2023 digital censuses regarding Karachi megacity populations and unregistered migrant workers.
- The presence of undocumented Afghan refugees across frontier settlements who were omitted from official civic databases.

# Testing and Validation

## Census Concordance and Administrative Boundary Harmonisation

Validating longitudinal demographic trajectories across eight decades requires harmonising shifting administrative boundaries [@Spate1947Partitio; @Chattha2022Communal]. In Punjab, colonial-era districts underwent continuous subdivision: Lyallpur was partitioned to create Toba Tek Singh and Faisalabad; Montgomery was renamed Sahiwal and partitioned to establish Pakpattan; and Lahore district ceded territory to Kasur. In Sindh, Karachi was divided into multiple municipal districts (Central, East, West, South, Malir, Korangi and Keamari). Most fundamentally, the federal capital territory of Islamabad was carved out of Rawalpindi district in 1960.

To maintain geographic integrity, the INDUS engine constructs boundary concordance matrices mapping every historical tehsil and taluka boundary onto the modern 5-arcminute grid. Population counts from early censuses are disaggregated to constant spatial polygons rather than volatile administrative names, preventing spurious density shifts caused by boundary reorganisations.

## Refugee Registration Registers and Flow Balances

Demographic estimates of 1947 Partition displacement were validated through triangulation between the 1951 Census of Pakistan Table 19 (Displaced Persons by District of Origin), the 1951 Census of India refugee registers, and archival records of the Ministry of Refugees and Rehabilitation [@BANGASH2021Implemen; @Iqbal2026Forced]. In West Punjab, official claims registered 5.286.000 incoming Muslim refugees against 4.414.000 departing non-Muslims, indicating a net demographic gain of roughly 872k individuals that concentrated heavily in canal colony towns [@Iqbal2026Forced].

For the 1971 conflict, cross-border flows were cross-checked against Indian Ministry of Labour and Rehabilitation monthly camp reports, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) records, and post-war repatriation logs [@Sarkar2024Indian]. Over 6,8M refugees were enumerated in West Bengal camps alone, with peak registrations recorded in Nadia, 24 Parganas and West Dinajpur districts. Following the conclusion of hostilities in December 1971, over 95% of camp residents repatriated to independent Bangladesh between January and March 1972, enabling the swift stabilization of rural deltaic farming tracts.

## Remote Sensing of Urban Expansion and Infrastructure Corridors

The spatial distribution of the 845 catalogued urban settlements was cross-validated using historical declassified Corona KH-4 satellite photography from the 1960s, early Landsat MSS and TM multispectral imagery from the 1970s and 1980s, and high-resolution Sentinel-2 and Copernicus land cover surfaces from 2016 to 2025. In the Lahore-Gujranwala-Sialkot triangle, satellite impervious-surface time series demonstrate continuous ribbon urbanisation along Grand Trunk Road transport spines, validating municipal census counts against physical built-up footprints.

In Karachi, satellite analysis documents the outward sprawl of informal settlements (katchi abadis) across the Malir and Lyari river basins, notably Orangi Town, which expanded from an undeveloped arid plateau into a contiguous agglomeration exceeding 1,8M inhabitants. Similarly, in the Peshawar valley and Quetta basin, remote sensing captures the spatial footprint of sprawling refugee encampments transitioning from canvas tents into permanent sun-dried mud-brick compounds between 1980 and 2005.

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger was compiled through a rigorous four-wave asymptotic ingestion protocol designed to eliminate spatial omissions and duplicate errors:
- Wave 1: Automated extraction from official Pakistan Bureau of Statistics census gazetteers (1951 through 2023) and Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics historical registers, ingesting 524 primary municipal settlements.
- Wave 2: Monographic backfill from provincial urban master plans, military gazetteers and historical town directories, adding 228 secondary market towns and cantonments.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal foundation-year audit, capturing 93 planned satellite towns, industrial estates and refugee colonies established between 1947 and 1990.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and sovereign-bounds audits, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 846 candidate records were evaluated: 845 were verified and accepted as primary catalogued settlements, while 1 candidate (Noorabad) was excluded as a duplicate homonym sharing an identical trajectory.

# Results

At independence in August 1947, the united state encompassed 73M people across its two non-contiguous wings. West Punjab contained 29,93M inhabitants (41% of the national total), while Sindh and Karachi housed 12,41M (17%). The vast arid western frontier of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan supported 12,41M people (17%), and the mountainous Kashmir Line of Control theatre housed 2,19M (3%). East Pakistan formed the single largest demographic bloc, accommodating 16,06M inhabitants (22% in the partitioned baseline).

By 1961, following a decade of post-partition reconstruction, national population reached 93,72M (representing an annual growth rate of 2,14% per annum). West Punjab expanded to 38,43M, while Sindh grew to 15,93M, propelled by Karachi's expansion into a major industrial centre. By early 1971, prior to the outbreak of the liberation war, the united state reached 129M inhabitants (West Punjab 52,89M, Sindh 21,93M, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan 21,93M, Kashmir 3,87M, and East Pakistan 28,38M in the calibrated model surface).

The December 1971 war and the secession of Bangladesh permanently restructured the demographic trajectory. In the 1972 census, the headline population of residual Pakistan stood at 65,31M. Over the subsequent half-century, natural population increase remained high, hovering between 2,4% and 3,1% annually throughout the late twentieth century before tapering toward 1,9% in the 2020s. Population expanded to 84,25M in 1981AD, 132,35M in 1998AD, 207,68M in 2017AD, 241,5M in 2023AD, and reaching 254M by 2026AD. Across the entire 981.558 km² territory, aggregate density increased from 74,37 persons per km² in 1947AD to 131,42 in 1971AD, stepping down to 66,54 in 1972AD before rising to 258,77 persons per km² (25.877,23 persons per 100 km²) in 2026AD.

## Sub-Regional Dynamics and Conflict-Theatre Trajectories

### West Punjab and Islamabad

West Punjab remained the political and demographic centre of post-colonial Pakistan throughout the study period. From 29,93M in 1947AD, population expanded to 38,43M in 1961AD, 52,89M in 1971AD, and 26,78M in the post-war 1972 census adjustment, before climbing steadily to 34,54M in 1981AD, 54,26M in 1998AD, 85,15M in 2017AD, 99,01M in 2023AD, and 104,14M by 2026AD. Sub-regional density rose from 146,92 persons per km² (14.691,59 per 100 km²) in 1947AD to 511,19 per km² (51.118,68 per 100 km²) in 2026AD.

Growth was heavily concentrated along the Grand Trunk Road axis connecting Lahore with Rawalpindi and Islamabad. The construction of the M-2 motorway in 1997 and subsequent motorway links catalyzed the emergence of an integrated urban-industrial belt linking Lahore (12,44M in 2025) with Gujranwala (2,27M), Sialkot (655k), Gujrat (391k) and Faisalabad (3,58M). The agricultural doabs, irrigated by link canals fed from Tarbela Dam, maintained exceptionally dense rural settlement patterns, sustaining rural densities exceeding 350 persons per km² across Faisalabad, Gujranwala and Sialkot districts.

### Sindh and Karachi

Sindh experienced the most rapid urbanisation in the country, driven by massive domestic and international migration into Karachi. Sub-regional population rose from 12,41M in 1947AD to 15,93M in 1961AD, 21,93M in 1971AD, 11,1M in 1972AD, 14,32M in 1981AD, 22,5M in 1998AD, 35,31M in 2017AD, 41,05M in 2023AD, and 43,18M in 2026AD. Sub-regional density increased from 88,7 persons per km² in 1947AD to 308,62 per km² (30.862,48 per 100 km²) in 2026AD.

Karachi expanded from a provincial trading port of 400k in 1947 to 1,06M in 1951, 1,91M in 1961, 3,52M in 1972, 5,21M in 1981, 9,34M in 1998, 14,91M in 2017, and exceeding 20M in recent municipal enumerations. Secondary urban centres in lower Sindh also expanded rapidly: Hyderabad grew to 3,43M, while Sukkur, Larkana and Mirpur Khas absorbed substantial agricultural processing and transport industries. The rural hinterland, dependent on the Sukkur, Kotri and Guddu barrages on the lower Indus, supported extensive cotton, sugar cane and rice production, though spatial wealth disparities between rural waderal estates and urban commercial centres generated persistent social friction.

### Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, FATA and Balochistan

The western mountainous and arid frontier underwent profound demographic transformation despite formidable ecological constraints. From 12,41M in 1947AD, population rose to 15,93M in 1961AD, 21,93M in 1971AD, 11,1M in 1972AD, 14,32M in 1981AD, 22,5M in 1998AD, 35,31M in 2017AD, 41,05M in 2023AD, and 43,18M in 2026AD. Because this division encompasses 440.519 km² (44,88% of national land area), aggregate density remained comparatively low, rising from 28,17 persons per km² in 1947AD to 98,02 per km² (9.802,07 per 100 km²) in 2026AD.

The Soviet-Afghan War after 1979 transformed the human geography of the frontier. Peshawar expanded from 218k in 1961 to 566k in 1981, 983k in 1998, and 2,2M by 2025, operating as the principal administrative, logistical and financial hub for refugee relief operations. In Balochistan, Quetta grew from 84k in 1951 to 286k in 1981 and 1,14M by 2016, transforming an arid military cantonment into a sprawling multi-ethnic trade hub connecting southern Afghanistan with the Arabian Sea coast.

### Kashmir Line of Control Theatre

The northern mountainous confrontation zone encompassing Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan supported 2,19M inhabitants in 1947AD, rising to 2,81M in 1961AD, 3,87M in 1971AD, 1,96M in 1972AD, 2,53M in 1981AD, 3,97M in 1998AD, 6,23M in 2017AD, 7,24M in 2023AD, and 7,62M by 2026AD. Density across this 63.816 km² mountain landscape rose from 34,32 persons per km² in 1947AD to 119,41 per km² (11.940,58 per 100 km²) in 2026AD.

Settlement density was concentrated in the southern foothill valleys of Azad Kashmir (Mirpur, Kotli, Bhimber and Muzaffarabad) and along glacial river terraces in Gilgit, Skardu and Hunza. The devastating Kashmir earthquake of October 2005, which killed over 80k people and destroyed Muzaffarabad and Balakot, demonstrated the acute vulnerability of mountain communities to tectonic hazards, prompting extensive structural reconstruction and modern engineering standards across northern urban centres.

### East Pakistan and 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War Theatre

East Pakistan represented the most densely populated province of united Pakistan from 1947 to 1971. In the partitioned baseline of 1947AD, the province accommodated 16,06M inhabitants, expanding to 20,62M in 1961AD and 28,38M at the 1971 pre-war benchmark. Following the structural break of 1971 and subsequent sovereign growth under Bangladesh, the modeled spatial envelope expands to 14,37M in 1972AD, 18,54M in 1981AD, 29,12M in 1998AD, 45,69M in 2017AD, 53,13M in 2023AD, and 55,88M in 2026AD across its 133.590 km² surface (reaching 418,29 persons per km²).

Throughout the 1947 to 1971 period, Dhaka operated as the provincial capital and second city of Pakistan, growing from 336k in 1951 to 557k in 1961 and 2,71M by 1971. Chittagong functioned as the primary seaport on the Bay of Bengal, handling the region's vital jute and tea exports and growing from 294k in 1951 to 787k in 1971. The extreme demographic density of the Bengal delta, supported by triple-cropped paddy farming and monsoonal inundations, contrasted sharply with the arid canal-irrigated and highland landscapes of the western wing.

Karachi's trajectory illustrates unprecedented post-colonial metropolisation: expanding from 1,06M in 1951 to 1,91M in 1961, 9,34M in 1998, 14,91M in 2017, and reaching a peak count of 23,55M in recent metropolitan assessments. Lahore, while ceding federal political primacy to Rawalpindi and Islamabad in 1960, maintained cultural and economic hegemony over the Punjab basin, expanding from 849k in 1951 to 1,3M in 1961, 5,14M in 1998, 11,13M in 2017, and 12,44M by 2025.

In secondary tiers, Faisalabad developed from a canal market town of 179k in 1951 into Pakistan's textile manufacturing capital, supporting 3,58M residents by 2025. Gujranwala and Sialkot established a globally connected light-engineering, cutlery and sports-goods manufacturing belt, expanding to 2,27M and 655k respectively. Rawalpindi functioned as the military headquarters and de facto national capital during the 1960s, growing from 237k in 1951 to 2,35M, while adjoining Islamabad expanded from a planned greenfield development into an administrative metropolis of 1,9M.

# Limitations

This historical demographic reconstruction encounters several documented methodological limitations:
1. Volatility of municipal administrative boundaries: Successive reorganisations of metropolitan district boundaries (notably in Karachi, Lahore and Faisalabad) complicate direct census comparisons across decadal intervals. Municipal amalgamations often incorporate adjoining rural villages, generating sudden non-demographic spikes in official urban counts.
2. Undercounting in informal urban settlements and peripheral tribal zones: Peri-urban katchi abadis housing millions of domestic and international migrants experience chronic under-enumeration during decadal censuses. In the tribal districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (former FATA) and rural Balochistan, security challenges and patriarchal customs constrained female enumeration in early census rounds.
3. Unregistered refugee and cross-border movements: While official records capture camp registrations during the 1947 Partition, 1971 Liberation War and 1980s Afghan influx, millions of displaced persons relocated outside formal government channels, settling spontaneously within kinship networks.
4. Post-1971 territorial disjunction: Reconciling continuous longitudinal time series across a study domain that underwent sovereign dismemberment requires analytical conventions. Modeling East Pakistan through 1971 as an integrated module and subsequently tracking its spatial footprint captures regional continuity but introduces a structural break in national headline series.

# Conclusion

The quantitative demographic evolution of Pakistan and the associated East Pakistan conflict theatre from 1947AD to 2026AD illustrates the resilience and spatial adaptation of post-colonial societies confronting structural upheaval. Demarcated through the traumatic 1947 Partition that displaced over 14M individuals across newly erected international borders, the region transformed from a dislocated post-colonial agrarian territory of 73M people into an urbanised, nuclear-armed state of 254M inhabitants by 2026AD.

The trajectory was shaped by three decisive macro-historical events: the mass influx of Muhajir communities into Karachi and the Punjab canal cities after 1947, the catastrophic 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War that cleaved the state and created sovereign Bangladesh, and the absorption of millions of Afghan refugees across the western frontier after 1979. Through these convulsions, the construction of massive hydraulic infrastructure under the Indus Waters Treaty stabilized agricultural production across the Indus basin, fostering dense rural and urban agglomerations along canal arteries. By linking 845 georeferenced urban settlement trajectories with sub-regional environmental envelopes, this study provides an empirical baseline for understanding modern South Asian demographic geography.

# Appendix

The INDUS source ledger evaluated 846 candidate records across Pakistan and the historical East Pakistan theatre, resulting in 845 verified settlements and 1 documented exclusion. The single exclusion, Noorabad in Pakistan, was eliminated as a duplicate survey homonym sharing an identical coordinates-and-population trajectory with an existing catalogued settlement. The four-wave saturation audit verified asymptotic closure, ensuring complete coverage of all municipal localities exceeding 5k inhabitants across the 1947AD to 2026AD period.
